subject: St Jerome (Eusebius Hieronymus), about 347 to 420

text_used.text: Every English quotation of Jerome is checked word for word against the unrevised translation by W. H. Fremantle with G. Lewis and W. G. Martley (NPNF 2nd series, vol. 6, 1893), downloaded whole from CCEL, marked Public Domain. 'exact' is the text as printed there, footnote numbers taken out. 'display' applies the site's capitals rule (it changes nothing in this file: every pronoun for God in these lines is already capitalised). Rufinus and Jerome's Lives of Illustrious Men: NPNF2-03 (Fremantle, 1892). Augustine's letters: NPNF1-01 (Cunningham). Augustine's anti-Pelagian treatises: NPNF1-05. Sulpicius Severus (Roberts, 1894) and Cassian (Gibson, 1894): NPNF2-11. Palladius: W. K. Lowther Clarke, 1918. Latin lines are checked against Migne (PL 22 and 26, via catholiclibrary.org) or la.wikisource.
text_used.source: CCEL plain-text volumes, all marked Public Domain
text_used.note: New Advent's copy of the same translation is revised (thee/thou become you, some wording modernised). Some lines differ: the dream line is 'You lie, you are a follower of Cicero' at New Advent but 'Thou liest, thou art a follower of Cicero' in the 1893 print. The quiz's lines on the site were found word for word in the 1893 print too (checked). Chapter links: CCEL letter pages have the form npnf206.v.<Roman numeral>.html; every one used below was fetched (HTTP 200) and contains its line. New Advent letter pages are 3001NNN.htm.

born_place.text: Born at Stridon, a town 'on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia', which the Goths later destroyed. No one knows today exactly where it stood. Britannica gives three guesses: near Ljubljana (Slovenia), Zagreb (Croatia) or Zenica (Bosnia and Herzegovina). His parents were Christians and well off. His father was called Eusebius.
born_place.source: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men, chapter 135 (his own entry): 'I, Jerome, son of Eusebius, of the city of Strido, which is on the border of Dalmatia and Pannonia and was overthrown by the Goths'; Britannica ('born to well-to-do Christian parents at Stridon (probably near what is now Ljubljana, Slovenia; Zagreb, Croatia; or Zenica, Bosnia and Herzegovina)')
born_place.note: NPNF prolegomena: the Gothic invasion of 377 partly destroyed Stridon; his parents were Catholic Christians, 'but he was not baptised in infancy'. The site's quiz data says only 'Rome and Bethlehem' for where.

born_year.text: About 347. Older books say 340 to 345. The sources disagree.
born_year.source: Britannica ('born c. 347'); Merriam-Webster ('circa 347-419 (or 420)'); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 ('around 347'); Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('about the year 340-2'); NPNF2-06 prolegomena ('A.D. 345'); saint.gr ('345')
born_year.note: The NPNF2-03 footnote on Lives of Illustrious Men 135 even says 'Born 331'. Plain wording that holds: 'Born about 347 (older books say 340 to 345)'.

grew_up.text: At Stridon, then at school in Rome from about the age of 12. He studied grammar and rhetoric there under the grammarian Donatus, and was baptised in Rome as a young man, about 366.
grew_up.source: Britannica ('His education, begun at home, was continued in Rome when he was about 12 ... near the end of his Roman education was baptized (c. 366)'); Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, Book 1 ('my master Donatus on Virgil'); OCA ('When the youth was about 20 years old, he accepted holy Baptism')
grew_up.note: A human detail from Jerome himself (Apology 1.30): as a boy he was 'dragged like a captive from my grandmother's lap to the lessons of my enraged Orbilius' (Orbilius: Horace's proverbially harsh schoolmaster). The Catholic Encyclopedia says he went to Rome 'probably about 360'.
grew_up.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "famous" dropped; no fetched source calls Donatus famous (Jerome says only "my master Donatus", Apology 1; Fremantle: "studied rhetoric ... under Aelius Donatus").

died.text: Died 30 September 420, at Bethlehem, after a long illness. Some sources say 419.
died.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('died at Bethlehem, 30 September, 420'); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 ('until his death on September 30, 420'); Britannica ('died 419/420, Bethlehem'); NPNF2-06 prolegomena ('The last year of his life is believed to have been occupied by a long illness, in which he was tended by the younger Paula and Melania'); Jerome to Alypius and Augustine (Augustine's Letter 202, a.d. 419): 'I have suffered so much through the attacks of disease'
died.note: No eyewitness account of his death survives. The NPNF prolegomena says 'The Chronicle of Prosper of Aquitaine gives September 20, 420' (20 is probably a misprint for 30; Prosper's Latin was not found and is not checked). Hydatius, who as a small child saw Jerome, wrote that he could not learn when Jerome died (Chronicle, preface: 'Quo vero tempore sancti Joannes, Hieronymus ... obierint ... referentum sermo non edidit'). Wikipedia says Prosper gives his age as 91; not checked.
died.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the page no longer states "after a long illness" as fact. Fremantle: "The last year of his life is believed to have been occupied by a long illness". The page says "believed".

buried.text: At Bethlehem, near the cave of the Nativity, beside Paula and Eustochium. His body was later said to have been taken to Rome, to the basilica of St Mary Major. The OCA says the present place of his relics is unknown.
buried.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 ('buried in a chapel beneath the Church of the Nativity, near the traditional place of our Lord's birth'); The Roman Martyrology (1916), 30 September ('buried near the manger of our Lord. His body was afterwards conveyed to Rome, and deposited in the basilica of St. Mary the Greater') and 9 May ('At Rome, also, the translation of St. Jerome ... from Bethlehem of Juda, to the basilica of St. Mary of the manger'); NPNF2-06 prolegomena ('His remains are said to have been transferred ... to the Church of Santa Maria Maggiore'); OCA ('His relics were transferred from Bethlehem to Rome in 642, but their present location is unknown')
buried.note: The OCA's date 642 is not checked elsewhere. The textmanuscripts.com note (citing Rice, Saint Jerome in the Renaissance, 1985) says the remains 'were believed to have been transferred in the late thirteenth century'. So the date of the move is uncertain; say 'later said to have been taken to Rome'.

roles.text: Student in Rome: grammar and rhetoric, and a growing library.
roles.source: Britannica; Letter 22, section 30 ('the library which I had formed for myself at Rome with great care and toil')

roles.text: Hermit in the Syrian desert of Chalcis, about 375 to 377. There he began Hebrew.
roles.source: Letter 22, section 7; Letter 125, section 12; Britannica ('In 375 Jerome began a two-year search for inner peace as a hermit in the desert of Chalcis')
roles.note: The Catholic Encyclopedia and NPNF say 374 to 379. Britannica says two years. Say 'a few years'.

roles.text: Priest, ordained at Antioch by Bishop Paulinus, on condition that he stayed a monk. He never served a parish.
roles.source: Against John of Jerusalem, section 41 (his words to Paulinus); Britannica ('Jerome accepted (378) on two conditions'); NPNF prolegomena ('he then and always afterwards declined the active ministry')
roles.note: Year: 378 (Britannica, Lesser Feasts and Fasts) or 379 (NPNF).

roles.text: Secretary to Pope Damasus in Rome, 382 to 384. Damasus set him to revise the Latin Gospels.
roles.source: Letter 123, section 10 ('when I was helping Damasus bishop of Rome with his ecclesiastical correspondence'); Britannica; Britannica, 'Vulgate' ('In 382 Pope Damasus commissioned Jerome')
roles.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: secretary 382 to 384. Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022: "From 382 to 384, he served as secretary to Pope Damasus I"; Damasus died 11 December 384 (Catholic Encyclopedia). Britannica's 382-385 is his whole stay in Rome (he sailed in August 385).

roles.text: Monk and translator at Bethlehem, 386 to 420. He ran the men's monastery that Paula built, and translated the Old Testament from Hebrew.
roles.source: Britannica ('There, by 389, Paula finished a monastery for men under Jerome's direction ... Here Jerome lived, except for brief journeys, until his death'); Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Latin Versions of the Bible' (390 to 405)

also_called.text: Eusebius Hieronymus, his Latin name. 'Jerome' is the English form of Hieronymus.
also_called.note: OCA gives 'Eusebius Hieronymos Sophronius'. The name 'Sophronius' is common online but not in his own Lives of Illustrious Men entry; not used.

also_called.text: Jerome of Stridon (OCA: 'Saint Jerome (Hieronymus) of Stridon').
Blessed Jerome of Stridon, in the Russian Church ('Иероним Блаженный, Стридонский'; also 'Блаженный Иероним').
also_called.source: azbyka.ru, page title and life; the 1903-1911 Russian Lives of the Saints icon is captioned 'Блаженный Иероним'
also_called.note: The Russian Church gives the same title 'Blessed' to Augustine. The Kiev Theological Academy's Russian translation of his works (1879-1900) is titled 'Творения блаженного Иеронима Стридонского'. azbyka's text also calls him 'Прп.' (Venerable) and 'святой'.

also_called.text: The Venerable Jerome ('Όσιος Ιερώνυμος') in the Greek synaxaria.

catholic.text: 30 September, a memorial in the General Roman Calendar ('Memorial of Saint Jerome, Priest and Doctor of the Church'). The 1916 Roman Martyrology also keeps 9 May, the moving of his body from Bethlehem to St Mary Major in Rome.
catholic.source: USCCB readings page for 30 September 2025 (read in a browser; curl was blocked); The Roman Martyrology (1916), 30 September and 9 May
catholic.note: 1916 Martyrology, 30 September, exact: 'In Bethlehem of Juda, the decease of St. Jerome, priest and Doctor of the Church, who, excelling in all kinds of learning, imitated the life of the most approved monks, and disposed of many monstrous heresies with the sword of his doctrine. Having at length reached a very advanced age, he rested in peace, and was buried near the manger of our Lord.' The 9 May entry is in the Ninth Day of May. The current (2004) Martyrology was not checked.

orthodox.text: 15 June. The OCA and the Greek synaxaria keep 15 June. The Russian Church keeps 15 June on the old calendar, which is 28 June on the civil calendar.
orthodox.source: OCA ('Commemorated on June 15'); saint.gr ('Εορτάζει στις 15 Ιουνίου'); azbyka.ru ('День памяти 28 июня')
orthodox.note: In the Greek calendar he shares 15 June with the prophet Amos and Augustine of Hippo (saint.gr day image: 'Προφήτης Αμώς, Όσιος Ιερώνυμος, Άγιος Αυγουστίνος'). The OCA also keeps 'Blessed Augustine' on 15 June. GOARCH could not be checked: goarch.org answered with a security check, which I did not get round.

old_calendar_note.text: Churches on the old (Julian) calendar keep 15 June on what is 28 June on today's calendar.
old_calendar_note.source: azbyka.ru gives 28 June; the 13-day gap holds from 1900 to 2099

anglican.text: 30 September. A Commemoration in the Church of England ('Jerome, Translator of the Scriptures, Teacher of the Faith, 420'), and kept in the Episcopal Church ('Jerome, Priest and Scholar, 420').
anglican.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar (printed in italics, which marks a Commemoration: the page says 'Commemorations are printed in italics'); The Episcopal Church, Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, calendar (September) and pp. 442-443
anglican.note: Raw HTML saved (coe-calendar-markup.txt): '30 ... Jerome, Translator of the Scriptures, Teacher of the Faith, 420'. Martin is a Lesser Festival there; Jerome is only a Commemoration. Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 PDF: https://www.episcopalchurch.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/Lesser-Feasts-and-Fasts-2022_final.pdf

lutheran.text: 30 September. Missouri Synod: 'Jerome, Translator of Holy Scripture'. ELCA: 'Jerome, translator, teacher, died 420'.
lutheran.source: LCMS, Commemorations list (September); ELCA: the Grand Canyon Synod of the ELCA's 'For What Shall We Pray?' page lists 'Jerome, translator, teacher, died 420 (Sept 30)'; Evangelical Lutheran Worship, The Church Year, assembly version, January 2006 (ELCA / Augsburg Fortress), September: "30 Jerome, translator, teacher, 420 W"
lutheran.note: The ELCA wording is checked only on an ELCA synod's page, not in an ELCA churchwide document. ELCA's 'What is a Commemoration' PDF does not list names.
lutheran.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: ELCA now confirmed in an ELCA churchwide book, Evangelical Lutheran Worship (2006), https://web.archive.org/web/20060908112753/http://www.renewingworship.org/ELW/content/PDF/ChurchYear_asm_20060119.pdf (HTTP 200, application/pdf). Text copied to sources/people/jerome/elw-churchyear-2006.txt from sources/people/ambrose-of-milan/elw-churchyear.txt.

why_dates_differ.text: The West keeps the day he died, 30 September. No source I found says why the East keeps 15 June.
why_dates_differ.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (died 30 September 420); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022
why_dates_differ.note: Not verified: any explanation of the Eastern 15 June.

status.text: A saint in the Catholic and Orthodox churches, and remembered by Anglicans and Lutherans. For Catholics he is a Doctor of the Church, one of the four great Latin Doctors with Ambrose, Augustine and Gregory the Great.
status.source: USCCB ('Priest and Doctor of the Church'); Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Doctors of the Church' ('In the Western church four eminent Fathers of the Church attained this honour in the early Middle Ages ... a decree of Boniface VIII (1298) ordering their feasts to be kept as doubles in the whole Church'); OCA; saint.gr; azbyka.ru; Church of England; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; LCMS

patron_of.text: Translators, Bible scholars, librarians, students and archaeologists (Britannica). The UN chose his feast day, 30 September, as International Translation Day.
patron_of.source: Britannica ('St. Jerome is the patron saint of Biblical scholars, librarians, students, translators, and archaeologists'); United Nations ('30 September celebrates the feast of St. Jerome, the Bible translator, who is considered the patron saint of translators'; General Assembly resolution 71/288, adopted 24 May 2017)
patron_of.note: The UN page also calls him 'a priest from North-eastern Italy' and says he 'translated parts of the Hebrew Gospel into Greek'; neither is used. Neither the Catholic Encyclopedia nor the 1916 Martyrology names a patronage for him (the scanned Martyrology's patron list is cut off by a page break).

in_art.text: With a lion at his side. This comes from a legend (see Often misquoted).
in_art.source: Anna Jameson, Sacred and Legendary Art, vol. 1 (1870 edition, Project Gutenberg): 'attended by a lion'

in_art.text: In a cardinal's red hat and robes, or with the red hat at his feet. There were no cardinals in his day.
in_art.source: Jameson: 'there is no historical authority for making St. Jerome a cardinal'
in_art.note: Both pictures chosen for the page show it: El Greco's cardinal's robes, and the hat on the ground in the Ravenna icon.

in_art.text: As a penitent in the wilderness: half naked, kneeling before a crucifix, beating his breast with a stone, often with a skull.
in_art.source: Jameson ('St. Jerome, half naked, emaciated ... beating his breast with a stone ... at his feet are a skull and hour-glass'); the breast-beating is his own (Letter 22, section 7: 'ceased not from beating my breast')
in_art.note: The stone is the painters' addition. Letter 22 mentions only beating his breast.

in_art.text: As a scholar at his desk with book and pen.
in_art.source: Jameson ('usually seated in a cave or in a cell, busied in reading or in writing')

wrote.text: The Latin Bible later called the Vulgate: he revised the Gospels and translated most of the Old Testament from Hebrew. Also commentaries on the prophets and on other books of the Bible, Lives of three hermits (Paul, Malchus, Hilarion), Lives of Illustrious Men (135 short lives of Christian writers, ending with himself), a translation and continuation of Eusebius's world chronicle, fierce answers to his opponents, and about 120 surviving letters.
wrote.source: Catholic Encyclopedia 1910 ('The correspondence of St. Jerome ... comprises about one hundred and twenty letters from him, and several from his correspondents'); Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Latin Versions of the Bible'; Britannica, 'Vulgate'; Lives of Illustrious Men 135
wrote.note: OCA: 'About 120 letters, considered as authentically written by Saint Jerome, have been preserved.' The research file's 'about 125' has no source; use about 120.
wrote.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "most of the Bible" overstated. The Catholic Encyclopedia lists commentaries on the prophets, Ecclesiastes and four of Paul's letters (and Matthew is known), not most of the Bible.

pronounced.text: juh-ROHM (also JERR-um). His Latin name, Hieronymus: hy-uh-RON-uh-mus.
pronounced.source: Merriam-Webster: 'Je·rome jə-ˈrōm, also ˈjer-əm'; 'Eusebius Hieronymus ˌhī-ə-ˈrä-nə-məs'

numbers.text: 34: years he lived at Bethlehem, from 386 until he died in 420.
numbers.source: Britannica ('The summer of 386 found him settled in Bethlehem'); Catholic Encyclopedia (died 420); azbyka.ru ('Последние 34 года жизни провёл в Вифлееме', the last 34 years of his life he spent in Bethlehem)

numbers.text: 15: years he spent translating the Old Testament from Hebrew, from 390 to 405.
numbers.source: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Latin Versions of the Bible' ('He set himself to the task A.D. 390 and in A.D. 405 completed the protocanonical books of the Old Testament from the Hebrew'); Britannica, 'Vulgate' ('completing the process c. 405')

numbers.text: About 120: letters of his that survive.
3: languages he worked in, Latin, Greek and Hebrew. A visitor said no one dared compare himself with him.
numbers.source: Sulpicius Severus, Dialogues, Dialogue I, chapter 8 ('a man learned not only in Latin and Greek, but also Hebrew, to such a degree that no one dare venture to compare himself with him in all knowledge')

numbers.text: 135: short lives in his Lives of Illustrious Men. The last one is about himself.
About 3: years in Rome as Damasus's man before the city turned on him ('almost three years').
numbers.source: Letter 45, section 2 ('Such is the company in which I have lived for almost three years')

traits.trait: A fighter, and he said so
traits.text: He wrote that in an argument he stood 'in the thick of the fray'. He admitted his anger outright, and he gave opponents nicknames: Vigilantius ('Wakeful') became 'Dormitantius' ('Sleepy').

quotes.exact: I stand in the thick of the fray, my life in constant danger
quotes.display: I stand in the thick of the fray, my life in constant danger

quotes.exact: I will frankly admit that my indignation overpowers me; I cannot listen with patience to such sacrilegious opinions.
quotes.display: I will frankly admit that my indignation overpowers me; I cannot listen with patience to such sacrilegious opinions.

quotes.exact: All at once Vigilantius, or, more correctly, Dormitantius, has arisen
quotes.display: All at once Vigilantius, or, more correctly, Dormitantius, has arisen

traits.text: A visitor who lived with him for six months said he read and wrote day and night. In his own list of his works he said he could not count his letters to Paula and Eustochium, 'for I write daily'.

quotes.exact: He is always occupied in reading, always at his books with his whole heart: he takes no rest day or night; he is perpetually either reading or writing something.
quotes.display: He is always occupied in reading, always at his books with his whole heart: he takes no rest day or night; he is perpetually either reading or writing something.
quotes.place: Sulpicius Severus, Dialogues, Dialogue I, chapter 9 (Postumianus speaking)

quotes.exact: how many Letters I have written To Paula and Eustochius I do not know, for I write daily
quotes.display: how many Letters I have written To Paula and Eustochius I do not know, for I write daily

traits.text: He told a young woman plainly how he had fought his desires in the desert, starving and still thinking of Rome.

quotes.exact: I used to dread my very cell as though it knew my thoughts; and, stern and angry with myself, I used to make my way alone into the desert.
quotes.display: I used to dread my very cell as though it knew my thoughts; and, stern and angry with myself, I used to make my way alone into the desert.

quotes.exact: I do not blush to avow my abject misery
quotes.display: I do not blush to avow my abject misery

traits.trait: Tender in grief, and funny about himself
traits.text: He wept as he wrote of friends who died. He could also laugh at himself: an old man with a grey head and a dewlap 'like that of an ox'.

quotes.exact: As often as I try to express myself in words and to scatter the flowers of this encomium upon his tomb, my eyes fill with tears, my grief returns, and I can think of nothing but his death.
quotes.display: As often as I try to express myself in words and to scatter the flowers of this encomium upon his tomb, my eyes fill with tears, my grief returns, and I can think of nothing but his death.
quotes.place: Letter 60 (to Heliodorus, on the death of Nepotian), section 1

quotes.exact: Now, however, my head is gray, my brow is furrowed, a dewlap like that of an ox hangs from my chin
quotes.display: Now, however, my head is gray, my brow is furrowed, a dewlap like that of an ox hangs from my chin

quotes.exact: I often seem in my dreams to be standing, a curly youth, dressed in my toga, to declaim a controversial thesis before the master of rhetoric; and, when I wake, I congratulate myself on escaping the peril of making a speech.
quotes.display: I often seem in my dreams to be standing, a curly youth, dressed in my toga, to declaim a controversial thesis before the master of rhetoric; and, when I wake, I congratulate myself on escaping the peril of making a speech.

others_on_him.exact: The heretics hate him, because he never desists from attacking them; the clerics hate him, because he assails their life and crimes. But beyond doubt, all the good admire and love him
others_on_him.display: The heretics hate him, because he never desists from attacking them; the clerics hate him, because he assails their life and crimes. But beyond doubt, all the good admire and love him
others_on_him.who: Postumianus, who stayed six months with him at Bethlehem, in Sulpicius Severus's Dialogues (about 404)
others_on_him.note: Roberts's text reads 'Hieronymus' for Jerome here. Postumianus goes on: 'the knowledge of the man is Catholic, and ... his doctrine is sound.'

others_on_him.exact: Jerome, the Teacher of the Catholics, whose writings shine like divine lamps throughout the whole world
others_on_him.display: Jerome, the Teacher of the Catholics, whose writings shine like divine lamps throughout the whole world
others_on_him.place: On the Incarnation of the Lord, Book 7, chapter 26
others_on_him.who: John Cassian, writing about 430, ten years after Jerome died

others_on_him.exact: we bless God that to yourself, to us, to all who read your works, He has given you as you are.
others_on_him.display: we bless God that to yourself, to us, to all who read your works, He has given you as you are.
others_on_him.who: Augustine of Hippo, writing to him before they had met

others_on_him.exact: A certain Jerome, a priest, distinguished Latin writer and cultivated scholar as he was, showed qualities of temper so disastrous that they threw into the shade his splendid achievements.
others_on_him.display: A certain Jerome, a priest, distinguished Latin writer and cultivated scholar as he was, showed qualities of temper so disastrous that they threw into the shade his splendid achievements.
others_on_him.who: Palladius, a hostile witness (a friend of Rufinus), writing about 420
others_on_him.note: The translator's footnote: 'Palladius' unfavourable opinion of Jerome was reciprocated'. Use only beside a friendly voice, and name him as a critic. Lowther Clarke's translation (1918) is public domain in the US.

life_moments.text: Rome, 360s. The student and his books. Jerome came to Rome as a boy to study. He built up a library 'with great care and toil', and he was baptised there as a young man.
life_moments.source: Letter 22, section 30; Britannica (Rome at about 12; baptised c. 366)
life_moments.note: Title: 'A student in Rome'. The NPNF prolegomena adds that he visited the martyrs' tombs in the catacombs on Sundays (Commentary on Ezekiel 40:5); that commentary passage is not in the fetched texts, so it is not checked.

life_moments.text: Antioch, about 375. The dream. Sick with fever in Lent, close to death, he dreamed he stood before the Judge. Asked who he was, he said 'I am a Christian.' The answer came: 'Thou liest, thou art a follower of Cicero and not of Christ.' He was flogged, and swore never to read pagan books again. He woke, he said, with bruised shoulders. Years later his old friend Rufinus called him a perjurer for still quoting the classics. Jerome answered that he had promised about the future, not wiped his memory.
life_moments.source: Letter 22 (to Eustochium), section 30; Rufinus, Apology against Jerome, Book 2, section 7; Jerome, Apology against Rufinus, Book 1, section 30
life_moments.note: Date: Britannica says mid-Lent 375 at Antioch; NPNF says 374. Jerome says only 'about the middle of Lent' on his way to Jerusalem. The Judge is 'He who presided'; Rufinus says outright 'The Lord Jesus Christ sits on the tribunal as judge'.
life_moments.title: The dream

quotes.exact: Thou liest, thou art a follower of Cicero and not of Christ.
quotes.display: Thou liest, thou art a follower of Cicero and not of Christ.

quotes.exact: I profess that my shoulders were black and blue, that I felt the bruises long after I awoke from my sleep
quotes.display: I profess that my shoulders were black and blue, that I felt the bruises long after I awoke from my sleep

quotes.exact: it was a promise for the future, not the abolition of my memory of the past
quotes.display: it was a promise for the future, not the abolition of my memory of the past

life_moments.text: Desert of Chalcis, about 375 to 377. Hebrew in the desert. Alone in the Syrian desert, burnt by the sun and fasting hard, he still could not stop thinking of girls and the pleasures of Rome. To tame his mind he asked a converted Jew to teach him Hebrew. After Cicero's smooth Latin, he had to learn 'words both harsh and guttural'. That Hebrew later made his Bible possible.
life_moments.title: Hebrew in the desert

quotes.exact: I often found myself amid bevies of girls
quotes.display: I often found myself amid bevies of girls

quotes.exact: But I thank the Lord that from this seed of learning sown in bitterness I now cull sweet fruits.
quotes.display: But I thank the Lord that from this seed of learning sown in bitterness I now cull sweet fruits.

life_moments.text: Rome, 382 to 385. Damasus's secretary, and the storm. Pope Damasus used him to answer letters and set him to revise the Latin Gospels. He taught Scripture and Hebrew to a circle of Roman women, Marcella and Paula among them. When Paula's daughter Blaesilla died of a fever at twenty, people in the crowd at her funeral whispered that fasting had killed her, and blamed the monks. Damasus died in December 384. In August 385 Jerome sailed from Rome, writing that people had called him 'an infamous turncoat'.
life_moments.source: Letter 123, section 10; Letter 127, section 7; Letter 39, section 6; Letter 45, sections 2 and 6; Britannica (dates)
life_moments.note: NPNF's heading for Letter 39 says 'Written at Rome in 389 a.d.', which cannot be right (he left Rome in 385); give no year for Blaesilla's death. Letter 39, section 1 says she was 'a girl of twenty'.
life_moments.title: The Pope's secretary

quotes.exact: How long must we refrain from driving these detestable monks out of Rome? Why do we not stone them or hurl them into the Tiber?
quotes.display: How long must we refrain from driving these detestable monks out of Rome? Why do we not stone them or hurl them into the Tiber?
quotes.note: The crowd at the funeral, as Jerome reports it.

quotes.exact: I am said to be an infamous turncoat, a slippery knave, one who lies and deceives others by Satanic arts.
quotes.display: I am said to be an infamous turncoat, a slippery knave, one who lies and deceives others by Satanic arts.

quotes.exact: I write this in haste, dear Lady Asella, as I go on board, overwhelmed with grief and tears
quotes.display: I write this in haste, dear Lady Asella, as I go on board, overwhelmed with grief and tears

life_moments.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: Letter 39, section 1 says she died of a "burning fever"; section 6 says "whispers such as these were audible in the crowd ... She weeps for her daughter, killed with fasting". The crowd did not "turn on" anyone; people whispered. Secretary years are 382 to 384 (see quick_facts.roles).

life_moments.text: Bethlehem, 386 to 405. The Bible from the Hebrew. Paula built a monastery for men under Jerome, convents for women and a guesthouse. From 390 to 405 he translated the Old Testament from the Hebrew. Paula learned Hebrew so well she could chant the psalms in it. When one of his new readings (an 'ivy' for Jonah's gourd) was read out in a church in North Africa, the congregation made such an uproar that the bishop nearly lost his flock.
life_moments.source: Britannica; Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Latin Versions of the Bible'; Letter 108, section 27; Augustine, Letter 71, section 5; Jerome, Letter 75 (Augustine's numbering), section 22
life_moments.title: The Bible from the Hebrew

quotes.exact: she could chant the psalms in Hebrew and could speak the language without a trace of the pronunciation peculiar to Latin
quotes.display: she could chant the psalms in Hebrew and could speak the language without a trace of the pronunciation peculiar to Latin

quotes.exact: The man was compelled to correct your version in that passage as if it had been falsely translated, as he desired not to be left without a congregation,--a calamity which he narrowly escaped.
quotes.display: The man was compelled to correct your version in that passage as if it had been falsely translated, as he desired not to be left without a congregation,--a calamity which he narrowly escaped.

life_moments.text: Bethlehem, 410. Rome falls. News came that Alaric's Goths had taken Rome. His old friend Marcella was beaten and died soon after. He broke down as he dictated. Then refugees poured into Bethlehem, and he stopped his commentary on Ezekiel to look after them.
life_moments.source: Letter 127 (to Principia), sections 12 to 14; Commentary on Ezekiel, prefaces to Books 1, 3 and 7 (as given in NPNF2-06)
life_moments.title: Rome falls

quotes.exact: My voice sticks in my throat; and, as I dictate, sobs choke my utterance. The City which had taken the whole world was itself taken
quotes.display: My voice sticks in my throat; and, as I dictate, sobs choke my utterance. The City which had taken the whole world was itself taken

quotes.exact: the quiet of the monastery has been changed into the bustle of a guest house
quotes.display: the quiet of the monastery has been changed into the bustle of a guest house
quotes.place: Commentary on Ezekiel, preface to Book 7

quotes.display: the bright light of all the world was put out

life_moments.text: Bethlehem, 416. Fire at the monastery. Supporters of Pelagius attacked the Bethlehem monasteries, beat the monks and nuns, killed a deacon and burned the buildings. Jerome escaped to a strong tower.
life_moments.source: Augustine, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, chapter 66; NPNF2-06 prolegomena (the tower; 416-7)
life_moments.note: Augustine reports it as hearsay ('They are said...').
life_moments.title: Fire at the monastery

miracles.text: No early source says Jerome worked a miracle. Leave the miracles section out. The wonders told of him are later: the lion (a story first told of Abba Gerasimus of the Jordan), and letters on his death and miracles that claim to be by Eusebius of Cremona, Augustine and Cyril of Jerusalem but were written about 900 years later.
miracles.source: Jameson, Sacred and Legendary Art, vol. 1 (the lion legend 'invented to explain the symbol'); textmanuscripts.com catalogue note, citing Rice, Saint Jerome in the Renaissance (1985): the three letters 'were probably written in Rome at the end of the thirteenth or early in the fourteenth century'; Jerome's own account of his dream (Letter 22, section 30) is a vision told by himself, placed among the life moments
miracles.note: Jerome wrote about other people's miracles (Lives of Paul and Hilarion). He also said that in the desert he sometimes 'felt myself among angelic hosts' (Letter 22, section 7).

feature.exact: The City which had taken the whole world was itself taken
feature.display: The City which had taken the whole world was itself taken
feature.context: On hearing, at Bethlehem, that the Goths had taken Rome in 410.
feature.latin: Capitur Urbs, quae totum cepit orbem

feature_alternative.exact: Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.
feature_alternative.display: Ignorance of the Scriptures is ignorance of Christ.
feature_alternative.note: His most searched line. No public-domain English translation of this prologue was found, so the English is our own word-for-word rendering of the Latin (the quiz already marks its own translations). The Vatican's English of Leo XIII's Providentissimus Deus (1893) gives 'To be ignorant of the Scripture is not to know Christ' (saved as providentissimus-deus-1893-en.txt; that translation's copyright status is not checked). If the page must print only public-domain translations, use the Latin with 'in our words' beside it, or choose the feature line above.

lines.exact: Always have some work on hand, that the devil may find you busy.
lines.display: Always have some work on hand, that the devil may find you busy.
lines.context: Advice to a young monk. Latin: Facito aliquid operis, ut te semper diabolus inveniat occupatum (checked in PL 22). Often quoted as "Be always doing something, so that the devil finds you busy."

lines.exact: The friendship which can cease has never been real.
lines.display: The friendship which can cease has never been real.

lines.exact: The art of interpreting the scriptures is the only one of which all men everywhere claim to be masters.
lines.display: The art of interpreting the scriptures is the only one of which all men everywhere claim to be masters.
lines.context: On amateurs who think the Bible needs no study.

lines.exact: Of two imperfect things holy rusticity is better than sinful eloquence.
lines.display: Of two imperfect things holy rusticity is better than sinful eloquence.
lines.context: From the great stylist, to a young priest.

lines.exact: When the stomach is full, it is easy to talk of fasting.
lines.display: When the stomach is full, it is easy to talk of fasting.

lines.exact: What is praiseworthy is not to have been at Jerusalem but to have lived a good life while there.
lines.display: What is praiseworthy is not to have been at Jerusalem but to have lived a good life while there.
lines.context: From a man who lived at Bethlehem. Two years earlier (Letter 47) he had urged a friend to come on pilgrimage.

lines.exact: The scars of others should teach us caution.
lines.display: The scars of others should teach us caution.

lines.exact: I beseech you, reader, whoever you may be, to remember Jerome the sinner. He, if God would give him his choice, would much sooner take Paul's tunic with his merits, than the purple of kings with their punishment.
lines.display: I beseech you, reader, whoever you may be, to remember Jerome the sinner. He, if God would give him his choice, would much sooner take Paul's tunic with his merits, than the purple of kings with their punishment.

lines.context: The last lines of an early book, written in the desert.
lines.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "his first book" dropped. NPNF dates the Life of Paul to 374 or 375 in the desert, but Britannica puts his earliest known work (De septies percussa, Letter 1) and the lost Obadiah commentary in the same years at Antioch; "first" is not settled.

lines.display: Almost all bodily excellences alter with age, and while wisdom alone increases all things else decay.

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: He pulled a thorn from a lion's paw, and the lion lived at his monastery. TRUTH: A later legend. Nothing in Jerome's own writings or in anyone who knew him mentions it. The same story is told of Abba Gerasimus of the Jordan, and the two names were confused.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Jameson, Sacred and Legendary Art (tells the legend and calls the lion a symbol, 'and in later times, the legend invented to explain the symbol'); NPNF2-06 prolegomena ('His descriptions of hermit life in the desert no doubt gave rise to the tradition that he was always attended by a lion ... With such traditions a historical work must not be burdened.'); none of the fetched texts by or about him (NPNF 6, 3, 11, 1, 5) mentions it
misquoted_or_legend.note: The Gerasimus source is John Moschus, Spiritual Meadow, chapter 107 (early 7th century). No public-domain English text was fetched, so the Gerasimus link is not checked here; Britannica says only 'According to tradition'. A c. 1500 Greek icon on Commons shows Jerome with a later inscription naming him Gerasimos, which shows the confusion (File: 'Grecia, icona del cristo dei dolori tra i s. giovanni battista e girolamo, 1500 ca., con iscrizione Gerasimos più tarda.jpg'; not downloaded).
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the page no longer says "nothing he wrote mentions it, and neither does anyone who knew him" (no fetched source says so). It says "a legend that grew up after his death" (Fremantle: "Many legends sprung up around his memory").

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: He was a cardinal (the red hat and robes). TRUTH: There were no cardinals in the modern sense in his day. He was a priest and a papal secretary.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Jameson ('there is no historical authority for making St. Jerome a cardinal. Cardinal-priests were not ordained till three centuries later'); Letter 123, section 10 (secretary)
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "for three years a pope's secretary" changed to "for a few years": 382 to December 384.

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: 'Good, better, best. Never let it rest, till your good is better and your better is best.' TRUTH: Not found anywhere in his works. A modern rhyme, in print by 1897 with no link to him.
misquoted_or_legend.source: fauxtations.wordpress.com (2016), searched his works at CCEL; my own search of the NPNF Jerome volume and of NPNF2-03 found no 'good ... better ... best' and no 'never let it rest'
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "Not found anywhere in his works" overstated what the source did. Fauxtations searched the CCEL English texts of Jerome and a regex over them; it also says the misattribution "appears to have happened in the early 21st Century". The page now says so.

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: He coined 'Never look a gift horse in the mouth.' TRUTH: He used it, but as an old saying: 'as the common proverb goes'. It is the earliest known written use.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Commentary on Ephesians, Prologue (Migne PL 26): 'noli de gratuito munere judicare, et, ut vulgare proverbium est: Equi dentes inspicere donati'
misquoted_or_legend.note: 'Earliest known written use' rests on phrase histories (wordhistories.net and others) and is not checked; safer: 'he quotes it as a common proverb'.

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: He alone translated the whole Vulgate. TRUTH: He revised the Gospels and translated most of the Old Testament from Hebrew. The rest of the New Testament came from older Latin versions, which he may have lightly revised. Books such as Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and Maccabees were left in the Old Latin.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Britannica, 'Vulgate' ('The remainder of the New Testament was taken from older Latin versions, which may have been slightly revised by Jerome. Certain other books ... were included from older versions.'); Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Latin Versions of the Bible' ('the remaining deuterocanonical books ... just as they existed in the Itala')
misquoted_or_legend.note: Jerome himself said 'I translated the New Testament from the Greek' (Lives of Illustrious Men 135), and the 1910 Catholic Encyclopedia thought he 'probably' revised all of it. Keep 'may have lightly revised'.
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the list "Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and the Maccabees" is in no fetched source. Britannica says only "Certain other books found in the Septuagint ... were included from older versions". The page now says that, without the list.

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: 'Vulgate' means the Bible in the tongue of the common people. TRUTH: The name comes from 'editio vulgata', the common (widely used) edition. The Episcopal Church's own calendar book gets this wrong.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Britannica, 'Vulgate' ('from the Latin editio vulgata, "common version"'); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, p. 442 ('the vulgus tongue used by the common people ... hence the name of his translation')
misquoted_or_legend.note: Optional: gentle, but LFF's reason is not wrong that Latin was the everyday language; the point is where the name came from.
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the "truth" now rests on the Catholic Encyclopedia, Latin Versions of the Bible: Its title "Vulgate", indicating its common use, and belonging to the Old Latin until the seventh century, was firmly established in the thirteenth. Note that Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 itself gives the "vulgus tongue" explanation; the page does not name it as the myth's source.

misquoted_or_legend.text: CLAIM: The deathbed letters (Eusebius of Cremona on his last hours, 'Augustine' and 'Cyril' on his miracles). TRUTH: Written in Rome about 900 years after he died, probably at the end of the 13th century or early 14th century. They shaped the paintings of his Last Communion.
misquoted_or_legend.source: textmanuscripts.com catalogue note, citing Rice, Saint Jerome in the Renaissance (1985), pp. 49-50, 63, 218-19
misquoted_or_legend.note: A dealer's scholarly description, not a primary source. Jameson tells the Last Communion as part of his story; mark it as legend.
misquoted_or_legend.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: the page no longer says the last-communion scene "comes from" these letters or that they "shaped the many paintings of the scene": the dealer's note says the letters are on his death and miracles, that artists "represented them in their frescoes, paintings and manuscript illuminations", and that Cyril of Jerusalem lived c. 313-386. The page says that.

where_he_stood.text: 17 of the quiz's 23 statements are on record for him: 14 show a line and 3 are hidden. All 13 English lines were found word for word in the 1893 NPNF print; the 'rich' line is the site's own translation of the Latin.

rows.statement: A good hearty laugh is good for the soul.
rows.line: Leave to worldlings the privileges of laughing and being laughed at. One who is in your position ought to be serious.

rows.statement: Most of the time, it's better to say less.
rows.line: You love silence, meekness, privacy; he takes delight in talking and effrontery, in squares, and streets, and apothecaries' shops.

rows.statement: Wisdom is worth learning from anyone, even people who don't share your faith.
rows.line: Is it surprising that I too, admiring the fairness of her form and the grace of her eloquence, desire to make that secular wisdom which is my captive and my handmaid, a matron of the true Israel?

rows.statement: Anger at real wrongdoing can be a good thing.
rows.line: I will frankly admit that my indignation overpowers me; I cannot listen with patience to such sacrilegious opinions.

rows.statement: If you had to choose, you'd grow closer to God alone in quiet than among other people.
rows.line: Do I condemn a solitary life? By no means: in fact I have often commended it.

rows.statement: There's nothing wrong with being rich, as long as you use it well.
rows.line: So that common saying seems to me most true: a rich man is either unrighteous or the heir of an unrighteous man.
rows.place: Letter 120 (to Hedibia), answer to her first question
rows.latin: Unde et illa vulgata sententia mihi videtur esse verissima. Dives autem iniquus, aut iniqui haeres.
rows.note: The site marks this line as its own translation (own: true). NPNF gives only a summary of Letter 120 (the twelve questions; 'The date of the letter is 406 or 407 A.D.'; New Advent 3001120.htm, saved as newadvent-letter120.txt), so there is no public-domain English of the text. Migne's text reads 'Dives autem iniquus' (the proverb is usually printed 'Dives aut iniquus aut iniqui heres'); the site's English follows the usual reading. Jerome calls it a common saying ('vulgata sententia'), not his own. The page should say 'a common saying he agreed with'.

rows.statement: If someone you know is doing wrong, it's your job to tell them.
rows.line: If an apostle or a prophet, themselves immaculate, could speak thus with a clemency embracing all, how much more earnestly should a sinner like me plead with a sinner like you.

rows.statement: Even if you believe you'll see them again, it's right to weep openly for someone you've lost.
rows.work_on_site: Letter to Paula on the death of Blaesilla
rows.line: Yours are detestable tears, sacrilegious tears, unbelieving tears; for they know no limits, and bring you to the verge of death.

rows.statement: Nature can teach you as much about God as the Bible can.
rows.note: Hidden on the site (hide: true): scored but no line shown. Not checked here.

rows.statement: The best way to live is free of strong emotions, with only a steady peace inside.
rows.note: Hidden on the site (hide: true): scored but no line shown. Not checked here.

rows.statement: Your body is a friend to look after, not an enemy to fight.
rows.line: We do not expect that it will be so with us, but we look for increased vigour of soul which becomes stronger as the flesh grows weaker.

rows.statement: Miracles still happen today, just as they did in the Bible.
rows.line: Some may wonder at the miracles he worked, or his incredible fasting, knowledge, and humility. Nothing so astonishes me as his power to tread under foot honour and glory.

rows.statement: Some questions about God are better left alone.
rows.note: Hidden on the site (hide: true): scored but no line shown. Not checked here.

rows.statement: If you believe God is calling you, follow, even if your family begs you not to.
rows.line: Should your father prostrate himself on the threshold, trample him under foot and go your way.
rows.site_note: He wrote this as a young man. Years later he said he had decked that letter out with the flourishes of the schools.

site_note_check.text: The site's note ('Years later he said he had decked that letter out with the flourishes of the schools') is right: Letter 52, section 1, exact: 'I decked it out a good deal with the flourishes of the schools'.

rows.statement: A church should keep out people who openly live in serious wrongdoing.
rows.line: As in the ark there were all kinds of animals, so also in the Church there are men of all races and characters.

rows.statement: Becoming a better person is mostly down to your own effort.
rows.line: To will and to run are mine, but they will cease to be mine unless God brings me His continual aid.

rows.statement: In the end, God will save everyone.
rows.line: Let us not wait for the repentance of the devil; for this is a vain anticipation and one that will drag us into the deep of hell. Life must be sought or lost here.

friends_family_rivals.text: Paula: a Roman noblewoman who followed him to Bethlehem, built its monasteries and learned Hebrew. His eulogy of her is Letter 108. She died in 404.
friends_family_rivals.source: Letter 108, sections 1 and 27; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 (Paula and Eustochium, 28 September; 'until her death in 404')

friends_family_rivals.text: Eustochium: Paula's daughter, to whom he wrote Letter 22 on virginity. She ran the convent after her mother and died about 418.
friends_family_rivals.source: Letter 22; NPNF prolegomena ('the death of Eustochium in 418'); Jerome to Alypius and Augustine, 419 ('the falling asleep of your distinguished and holy daughter Eustochium')
friends_family_rivals.note: Lesser Feasts and Fasts gives 'c. 419' for her death.

friends_family_rivals.text: Marcella: a Roman widow who pressed him with questions on Scripture and would not simply accept his answers. After he left Rome, people went to her to settle Bible questions.

quote.exact: nor would she at once acquiesce in my explanations but on the contrary would dispute them; not, however, for argument's sake but to learn the answers
quote.display: nor would she at once acquiesce in my explanations but on the contrary would dispute them; not, however, for argument's sake but to learn the answers

friends_family_rivals.text: Pope Damasus: made him his secretary and set him to revise the Latin Bible.

Gregory of Nazianzus: his teacher at Constantinople. Jerome tells how Gregory dodged a hard question with a joke: 'I will tell you about it in church, and there, when all the people applaud me, you will be forced against your will to know what you do not know at all.'

quote.exact: I will tell you about it in church, and there, when all the people applaud me, you will be forced against your will to know what you do not know at all.
quote.display: I will tell you about it in church, and there, when all the people applaud me, you will be forced against your will to know what you do not know at all.

friends_family_rivals.text: Didymus the Blind: the Alexandrian scholar he went to hear when his own hair was already grey.
friends_family_rivals.source: Letter 84, section 3 ('Yet I went on to Alexandria and heard Didymus')

friends_family_rivals.text: Augustine of Hippo: they wrote to each other from about 394 until 419 and never met. The early letters were sharp: Jerome told the younger man not to challenge a veteran ('The tired ox treads with a firmer step'). The last were warm: Augustine was 'renowned throughout the whole world'.

quotes.exact: The tired ox treads with a firmer step.
quotes.display: The tired ox treads with a firmer step.

quotes.exact: desist from annoying an old man, who seeks retirement in his monastic cell
quotes.display: desist from annoying an old man, who seeks retirement in his monastic cell

quotes.exact: You are renowned throughout the whole world; Catholics revere and look up to you as the restorer of the ancient faith
quotes.display: You are renowned throughout the whole world; Catholics revere and look up to you as the restorer of the ancient faith

friends_family_rivals.text: Rufinus of Aquileia: his closest friend in youth. They fell out over Origen and attacked each other in books for years. Augustine wrote that if such friends could break, any friend might become an enemy.
friends_family_rivals.source: Letter 3, section 6; Rufinus, Apology against Jerome; Jerome, Apology against Rufinus; Augustine, Letter 73, section 6

quote.exact: where is the friend who may not be feared as possibly a future enemy, if the breach that we deplore could arise between Jerome and Rufinus?
quote.display: where is the friend who may not be feared as possibly a future enemy, if the breach that we deplore could arise between Jerome and Rufinus?

friends_family_rivals.text: Origen: he admired and translated him ('our Christian man of adamant'), then turned against his teaching. Later he said he had praised 'the commentator but not the theologian'.

quotes.exact: our Christian man of brass, or, rather, man of adamant
quotes.display: our Christian man of brass, or, rather, man of adamant

quotes.exact: I have praised the commentator but not the theologian
quotes.display: I have praised the commentator but not the theologian

friends_family_rivals.text: Ambrose of Milan: Jerome mocked a book on the Holy Spirit as 'flaccid and soft, sleek and pretty' without naming its author. Rufinus said the target was Ambrose.
friends_family_rivals.source: Jerome's preface to Didymus On the Holy Spirit, quoted in Rufinus, Apology against Jerome, Book 2, sections 24-25

quote.exact: all is flaccid and soft, sleek and pretty, picked out with the rarest colours
quote.display: all is flaccid and soft, sleek and pretty, picked out with the rarest colours

friends_family_rivals.text: Paulinian: his brother, twenty years younger. He sailed east with Jerome in 385. In 394 Epiphanius ordained him priest for the Bethlehem monks by force: he told his deacons "to seize him and to stop his mouth".
friends_family_rivals.source: OCA ('his younger sisters and his brother Paulinian'); NPNF prolegomena ('a brother, Paulinian, twenty years his junior'); Against John of Jerusalem, section 41; Fremantle, NPNF2-06 prolegomena ("Jerome sailed with Vincentius and with his brother Paulinian ... direct to Antioch"; "ordained against his will, and with the employment of force and even gagging"); Epiphanius to John of Jerusalem, 394, Jerome's Letter 51, section 1
friends_family_rivals.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "lived at Bethlehem" not kept: Against John of Jerusalem, section 41 (397) says Paulinian "lives at Cyprus: he sometimes comes to visit us". The quotation "to seize him and to stop his mouth" is in jerome.quotes.json.

friends_family_rivals.text: Pelagius: Jerome wrote against his teaching, and Pelagius's supporters were said to have burned the Bethlehem monasteries.
friends_family_rivals.source: Letter 133; Augustine, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, chapter 66

friends_family_rivals.text: Vigilantius: a priest from Gaul who criticised the honouring of relics and night vigils. Jerome renamed him 'Dormitantius', the Sleepy.
Jovinian: a monk who taught that virgins, widows and wives have equal merit. Jerome's reply was so harsh that his friends in Rome tried to keep it quiet.
Palladius: a monk and bishop, friend of Rufinus, who wrote that Jerome's temper spoiled his achievements and that he held Paula back by his jealousy.

hard_topics.text: He put virginity far above marriage and said so bluntly. Even his friends thought he went too far: Pammachius pulled copies of Against Jovinian from circulation. Jerome answered that he was only following Paul, and that he 'hazarded an inquiry' where Paul had laid down a rule. The same man took women seriously as scholars: he answered Marcella's hard questions for years and praised Paula's Hebrew. The Catholic Encyclopedia (1910) says he used 'disparaging expressions' about marriage 'for which he has given no satisfactory explanation'.

holder.exact: I praise wedlock, I praise marriage, but it is because they give me virgins. I gather the rose from the thorns, the gold from the earth, the pearl from the shell.
holder.display: I praise wedlock, I praise marriage, but it is because they give me virgins. I gather the rose from the thorns, the gold from the earth, the pearl from the shell.

holder.exact: If it is good not to touch a woman, it is bad to touch one
holder.display: If it is good not to touch a woman, it is bad to touch one

holder.exact: Marriage replenishes the earth, virginity fills Paradise.
holder.display: Marriage replenishes the earth, virginity fills Paradise.

holder.exact: He defines a dogma, I hazard an inquiry.
holder.display: He defines a dogma, I hazard an inquiry.

critics.display: Certain persons find fault with me because in the books which I have written against Jovinian I have been excessive (so they say) in praise of virginity and in depreciation of marriage

critics.display: I quite recognize the kindness and forethought which have induced you to withdraw from circulation some copies of my work against Jovinian.

critics.display: She was hindered by a certain Jerome from Dalmatia. For though she was able to surpass all, having great abilities, he hindered her by his jealousy, having induced her to serve his own plan.

also.display: No; my sex is my one crime

hard_topics.text: He was cruel in grief and in argument, and knew it. He called a grieving mother's tears 'detestable'. He said severity for God's honour is no cruelty. He wrote that in debate 'one argues as one pleases, saying one thing while one means another'. The Episcopal Church's calendar book sums it up: an 'irascible disposition, pride of learning, and extravagant promotion of asceticism'.

holder.display: Yours are detestable tears, sacrilegious tears, unbelieving tears; for they know no limits, and bring you to the verge of death.

holder.exact: There is no cruelty in regard for God's honour.
holder.display: There is no cruelty in regard for God's honour.

hard_topics.critics_context: The same article says Jerome studied with several Jews, naming Lyddaeus, Baranina (Bar Hanina) of Tiberias and an Aramaic teacher; that he kept studying with Jews "during the forty years that he lived in Palestine"; and that "Although other Church Fathers quote Jewish traditions none equal Jerome in the number and faithfulness of their quotations." It lists that he "curses and reviles them; takes pleasure in their misfortune". Fetched 2026-09-24.

hard_topics.text: He praised and translated Origen, then led the attack on Origenism. Rufinus accused him of turning on what he had praised; Jerome said he had praised the scholar, not the doctrine. The Catholic Encyclopedia judges that 'Rufinus was to blame' but that Jerome's 'attitude is not always above reproach'.
hard_topics.source: Letter 33, section 3; Letter 84, section 2; Catholic Encyclopedia 1910

how_he_died.text: In old age, after a long illness, at Bethlehem on 30 September 420. In his last known letter (419) he wrote that disease and the death of Eustochium had worn him down. His eyes had long been failing: he could no longer read Hebrew by lamplight. No one who was there wrote an account of his death. The famous scene of his last communion comes from a letter forged in the 13th or 14th century.
how_he_died.source: Jerome to Alypius and Augustine (Augustine's Letter 202, a.d. 419); Commentary on Ezekiel, preface to Book 7 (his eyes); NPNF2-06 prolegomena; Catholic Encyclopedia (date); textmanuscripts.com, citing Rice (the forged letter of 'Eusebius of Cremona')
how_he_died.note: Exact lines: 'I have suffered so much through the attacks of disease, and through the falling asleep of your distinguished and holy daughter Eustochium' (Letter 202, section 2); 'my eyes are growing dim with age ... I am quite unable to go through the Hebrew books with such light as I have at night' (Ezekiel, preface to Book 7). The 1916 Martyrology: 'Having at length reached a very advanced age, he rested in peace'. No last words are recorded in any early source.

is_he_a_saint.text: Yes, in the Catholic and Orthodox churches, and Anglicans and Lutherans keep his day. Catholics honour him as a Doctor of the Church and keep 30 September. The Orthodox keep 15 June: the OCA calls him Saint Jerome of Stridon, the Greek synaxaria the Venerable Jerome, and the Russian Church 'Blessed Jerome', the title it also gives Augustine. The Church of England remembers him on 30 September as a Commemoration, and so do the Episcopal Church and Lutherans of the Missouri Synod and the ELCA.
is_he_a_saint.source: USCCB; 1916 Roman Martyrology; Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Doctors of the Church'; OCA; saint.gr; azbyka.ru; Church of England Common Worship; Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022; LCMS; Grand Canyon Synod (ELCA)
is_he_a_saint.note: Say plainly what 'Blessed' is: a title in Russian usage. I found no source that says the Russian Church doubts his holiness; do not suggest it.

prayer_he_wrote.text: No prayer composed by him as a prayer was found in the checked texts. Two lines come close. His oath in the dream: 'Lord, if ever again I possess worldly books, or if ever again I read such, I have denied Thee.' And the end of the Life of Paul, asking the reader to 'remember Jerome the sinner'. The cry 'Have mercy upon me, O Lord' in the dream is a psalm, not his own.
prayer_he_wrote.source: Letter 22, section 30; Life of Paul the First Hermit, section 18
prayer_he_wrote.note: The 'Prayer of St Jerome' that circulates online ('O Lord, show Thy mercy to me and gladden my heart. I am like the man on the way to Jericho...') was not found in his works here; not checked further. Leave the prayer section out, or print the dream oath with its context.

what_to_read_first.text: Letter 22, to Eustochium (384): his most famous letter, with the desert and the dream. Strict and sometimes harsh on marriage; read it knowing that.
what_to_read_first.checker_note: Checker 2026-09-25: "his most famous letter" softened to "his famous letter" (NPNF: "Perhaps the most famous of all the letters"; LFF 2022: "Jerome's famous De custodia virginitatis").

what_to_read_first.text: Letter 125, to Rusticus (411): an old monk's advice to a young one, with how he learned Hebrew.
Letter 127, to Principia (412): the life of his friend Marcella and the fall of Rome.
The Life of Paul the First Hermit (about 375): short, strange and vivid, his first book.

what_to_read_first.text: His letters with Augustine (394 to 419): two great minds, first sparring, then friends.

personality_test.text: The site's own reading: Jerome is one of two saints on the card for The Forge ('Serious by nature, and at your best when there is something to do.'), with John Chrysostom. Card text: 'The great translator of the Bible was a fighter by his own account. He wrote that in an argument he threw himself into the thick of it.' Source line on the card: 'Jerome, Letter 48'.
personality_test.note: Checked: Letter 48, section 13 has 'I stand in the thick of the fray, my life in constant danger'. 'Threw himself into' is a little stronger than 'stand in'; suggested wording: 'He wrote that in an argument he stood in the thick of the fray.' Say it is the site's reading. The Forge's 'something to do' fits 'Always have some work on hand' (Letter 125, section 11). The live URL was not opened.

groups.text: fathers teachers monks. Keep 'fathers' and 'teachers' (a Church Father and one of the four great Latin Doctors). Add 'monks': he lived as a hermit and then as a monk at Bethlehem for 34 years, heading its monastery for men.
groups.source: Catholic Encyclopedia, 'Doctors of the Church'; Britannica (monastery at Bethlehem); Against John of Jerusalem 41 (he stayed a monk when ordained)
groups.note: The hint was 'fathers teachers'. Martin (a monk-bishop) is in 'monks', and Jerome is more a monk than Martin was. Not 'desert': the site's desert group is the Egyptian desert fathers, and Jerome's desert years were short and in Syria (a judgment call).

lived.text: 400s is defensible (he died in 420, and his greatest work, the Hebrew Old Testament, was finished in 405). But he was born about 347 and lived 53 of his 73 years in the 300s. The mock-up puts Chrysostom (349-407) in 400s and Ambrose (339-397) in 300s, so by that rule (the century he died in) keep '400s'.
lived.note: Hint confirmed by the mock-up's own rule; flag if the filter means 'when he was active'.

side.text: west. He wrote in Latin and served the Western church, but he lived his last 34 years in Bethlehem and is kept by the Orthodox on 15 June. 'west' is right for the filter; the page can say he lived in the East.

people.jerome.hook: 'Christ called him a follower of Cicero'. Jerome says 'He who presided' and 'the Judge', and his oath is to God ('I have denied Thee'). Rufinus names Christ as the judge. Fine as it stands.

Research file's genuine lines are New Advent's revised wording. The 1893 print differs in the dream ('Thou liest, thou art a follower of Cicero') and 'O wilderness, gladdened with God's especial presence!' (not 'special'). All other lines checked are the same in both.

writer_additions.text: Facts the page writer read in the fetched texts and used on design/saints-hub/pages/jerome.json that the research above did not list. Each was read in context in the named file; every quotation among them is in research/people/jerome.quotes.json and passes verify-quotes.mjs.

items.text: Before the dream he would fast "only that I might afterwards read Cicero"; his funeral was being prepared; he insisted "this was no sleep nor idle dream".
As a boy he was "dragged like a captive from my grandmother's lap" to his lessons (at home, before Rome); "even now that my head is gray and bald" he dreamed of school.
To Bishop Paulinus at his ordination: "Did I ask to be ordained by you?" He asked to keep the monastic state.
items.note: The page does NOT say he never had charge of a church: Sulpicius, Dialogue I, chapter 8, has Postumianus say "The presbyter Jerome rules the church of this place" (Bethlehem). The page says he lived as a monk to the end.

items.text: When Rome turned on him: "Have I taken any one's money? Have I not disdained all gifts, whether small or great?"
As Damasus's secretary he wrote "his answers to the questions referred to him by the councils of the east and west".
In 410 soldiers beat Marcella for gold she did not have; she died "after a few days".
Jerome's reply on Jonah's plant: the Hebrew word is neither gourd nor ivy; he put ivy "that I might not differ from all other translators".
items.source: Jerome to Augustine, Letter 75 in Augustine's letters, section 22

items.text: To the young Augustine: "do not because you are young challenge a veteran in the field of Scripture".

Letter 84, section 3 goes on after "those of the circumcision": "For up to the present day they persecute our Lord Jesus Christ in the synagogues of Satan." Baraninas came by night "by his fear of the Jews", "a second edition of Nicodemus".
The question Gregory of Nazianzus dodged was Luke's phrase "the second-first Sabbath".
Tobit, from the Aramaic ("Chaldee"), with a speaker of both languages: "one day's hasty labour".
items.source: Jerome's preface to Tobit and Judith, as given in NPNF 2-06

items.text: Vulgate: Gospels revised about 383; Psalms, Job and others first from the Septuagint; then he judged the Septuagint unsatisfactory and went to the Hebrew, finishing about 405; not accepted at once; complete Bibles in common use from the mid-6th century; "primarily translated by St. Jerome".
items.note: Not quoted on the page (Britannica is in copyright); paraphrased.

items.text: Buried "beside those of Paula and Eustochium, near the grotto of the Nativity"; the lion tradition came from "His descriptions of hermit life in the desert".
items.source: Fremantle, NPNF 2-06 prolegomena, Life of Jerome

items.text: "it was the Bible of the Middle Ages".
items.source: Fremantle, NPNF 2-06 prolegomena, on the Vulgate

items.text: In old age "it is only the voice of the brethren which enables me to master the commentaries of Greek writers".
items.source: Commentary on Ezekiel, preface to Book 7, as given in NPNF 2-06

items.text: The lion legend (thorn, the ass, the camels); the lion was a symbol "befitting St. Jerome, from his fervid, fiery nature", and "the legend invented to explain the symbol".
items.source: Jameson, Sacred and Legendary Art, vol. 1 (1870)

items.text: Paula and Eustochium "were Jerome's colleagues in this work and without them there would be no Vulgate" (entry for 28 September); Jerome "candid at times in admitting his failings, never ambitious for churchly honors".
items.source: Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, pp. 442 and the Paula and Eustochium entry
items.note: In copyright: paraphrased on the page, never quoted.

items.text: azbyka.ru heads him "Преподобный Иероним Блаженный, Стридонский" (Venerable) and calls him "святой".
The rhyme as the fact-check prints it: "Good, better, best, Never let it rest, Til your good is better, and your better best."
Nepotian was Heliodorus's nephew ("your reverend uncle, Heliodorus").
